title: Equity and Effectiveness of Groundwater Governance Policies
content:
Abstract

Groundwater depletion threatens the sustainability of irrigated agriculture worldwide, particularly in regions where aquifers provide the primary or only irrigation source. While many policies have been designed to reduce pumping, previous studies have emphasized hydrologic effectiveness or average regional economic outcomes, with less attention to how groundwater-policy costs and benefits are distributed among farmers. This study uses an agent-based modeling framework to systematically compare six groundwater governance approaches: uniform pumping restrictions, volumetric pumping fees with and without revenue recycling through groundwater conservation payments, two priority-based allocation systems, and a priority-weighted pumping restriction system. Across various climate and market conditions, we designed each policy to meet the same groundwater-stabilization goal, allowing a fair and direct evaluation of both aquifer dynamics and the distribution of farm-level profits. When each policy was set to meet a common groundwater stabilization goal, they created very different economic outcomes for farmers. Policies that apply the same allocation to all irrigators or scale allocations by seniority produced the most balanced results. Fee-based pumping generated consistent but uniformly lower profits, while recycling fees as payments to farmers who forgo irrigation improved profitability and equity. By contrast, policies that strictly enforce water-rights seniority created an economic divide: senior users with water access maintained high earnings while junior farmers had little or no access to irrigation water. These findings highlight that considering both sustainability and distributive economic consequences provides a stronger foundation for evaluating and designing groundwater management policies that balance aquifer conservation with the economic well-being of producers.
